questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Vitiligo is characterised by:
options: Depigmented macules with autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
questions.concept: Well-defined chalk-white macules that fluoresce under Wood lamp, often around orifices and over bony prominences, with associated thyroid disease, diabetes and pernicious anaemia. Sensation is normal, unlike leprosy.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Pigmentary Disorders

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: The most important differential of a hypopigmented patch in India that must be excluded is:
options: Leprosy, by testing sensation and examining nerves
questions.concept: An anaesthetic hypopigmented patch with thickened peripheral nerves indicates tuberculoid leprosy. Pityriasis alba and post-inflammatory hypopigmentation are other differentials, but only leprosy has sensory loss.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Melasma is characteristically:
options: Symmetrical brown facial pigmentation worsened by sun and hormones
questions.concept: Melasma affects the malar, centrofacial and mandibular areas of women, aggravated by pregnancy, oral contraceptives and ultraviolet light. Strict photoprotection is essential; hydroquinone and triple combination creams are used.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Pigmentary Disorders

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: The mainstay of medical treatment for limited stable vitiligo is:
options: Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors with phototherapy
questions.concept: Repigmentation arises from follicular melanocyte reservoirs, so hairy areas respond better than acral skin and lips. Narrowband UVB is used for extensive disease and surgical grafting for stable resistant patches.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Pigmentary Disorders

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Albinism results from:
options: A defect in melanin synthesis with a normal number of melanocytes
questions.concept: Oculocutaneous albinism, often from tyrosinase deficiency, causes white skin and hair with photophobia, nystagmus and reduced acuity. Rigorous sun protection is essential given the high risk of skin cancer.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Pigmentary Disorders

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Ichthyosis vulgaris is characterised by:
options: Fine fish-like scaling with hyperlinear palms, sparing the flexures
questions.concept: Filaggrin mutations impair barrier formation, causing dry scaly skin with prominent palmar markings and strong association with atopic dermatitis. Flexural sparing distinguishes it from other ichthyoses.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Cafe-au-lait macules numbering six or more, over 15 mm in an adult, suggest:
questions.concept: NF1 diagnostic criteria also include axillary or inguinal freckling, two or more neurofibromas, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, a distinctive bony lesion and an affected first-degree relative.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Ash-leaf macules and adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) with seizures indicate:
questions.concept: Tuberous sclerosis shows hypomelanotic ash-leaf macules best seen under Wood lamp, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas, cortical tubers with epilepsy, and renal angiomyolipomas and cardiac rhabdomyomas.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Epidermolysis bullosa is characterised by:
options: Blistering at sites of minor trauma from inherited defects in structural adhesion proteins
questions.concept: Simplex, junctional and dystrophic forms are defined by the level of split - intraepidermal, lamina lucida and sublamina densa respectively. Management is supportive with meticulous wound care and avoidance of friction.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Pigmentary disorders (vitiligo, melasma) & genodermatoses
questions.stem: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is particularly troublesome in Indian skin because:
options: Higher constitutive melanin means inflammation readily provokes lasting pigment change
questions.concept: Fitzpatrick types IV to VI pigment readily after acne, eczema or any dermatitis, so treating the underlying inflammation early and rigorous photoprotection matter more than depigmenting agents alone.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Pigmentary Disorders

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are distinguished by:
options: The percentage of body surface area with epidermal detachment - under 10 percent versus over 30 percent
questions.concept: SJS involves under 10%, overlap 10 to 30% and TEN over 30% detachment. Both are severe cutaneous adverse reactions with mucosal involvement, and mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Drug Reactions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: The drugs most commonly implicated in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and TEN include:
questions.concept: Cotrimoxazole, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, nevirapine, allopurinol and oxicam NSAIDs are the classic culprits. HLA-B*1502 predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS in South Asian populations.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Drug Reactions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: The single most important step in managing toxic epidermal necrolysis is:
options: Immediate withdrawal of the offending drug with supportive burns-unit care
questions.concept: Early withdrawal improves survival. Management mirrors burns care - fluid balance, temperature control, nutrition, wound care, ophthalmology input and infection surveillance. The role of steroids and IVIG remains debated.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Drug Reactions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: A fixed drug eruption is characterised by:
options: A well-defined dusky plaque recurring at exactly the same site on re-exposure
questions.concept: Fixed drug eruption recurs at identical sites, often lips, genitalia or hands, leaving post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Cotrimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracyclines and paracetamol are common causes.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Drug Reactions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: DRESS syndrome is characterised by:
options: Rash with fever, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy and internal organ involvement, appearing 2 to 6 weeks after the drug
questions.concept: The long latency distinguishes DRESS from other drug eruptions, and hepatitis, nephritis and myocarditis may persist after drug withdrawal. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol and dapsone are typical causes.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Drug Reactions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: The ABCDE criteria for suspecting melanoma stand for:
options: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter over 6 mm and Evolution
questions.concept: Any changing pigmented lesion warrants excision biopsy with a narrow margin for histology, followed by wide local excision guided by Breslow thickness. Incisional or shave biopsy is avoided.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Skin Tumours

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: Basal cell carcinoma most characteristically presents as:
options: A pearly nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasia on sun-exposed skin
A scaly plaque on the trunk
questions.concept: BCC arises on the face above a line from the angle of the mouth to the ear lobe, is locally invasive as a rodent ulcer but essentially never metastasises. Squamous carcinoma has everted edges and does metastasise.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Skin Tumours

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: Acral lentiginous melanoma is important in Indian patients because it:
options: Occurs on palms, soles and nail beds where it is easily missed and presents late
questions.concept: It is the commonest melanoma subtype in darker-skinned and Asian populations. Longitudinal melanonychia with Hutchinson sign of periungual pigment spread is an important warning sign.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Skin Tumours

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: The quantity of topical steroid needed is estimated using:
options: The fingertip unit, approximately 0.5 g covering two adult palm areas
questions.concept: One fingertip unit is the amount from the distal crease to the fingertip of an adult index finger. This standardises prescribing, prevents both underuse from steroid phobia and overuse causing atrophy.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e, Topical Therapy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.topic: Drug reactions (SJS/TEN), skin tumours & melanoma; topical therapy
questions.stem: Topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus are valuable because they:
options: Provide steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory action without causing skin atrophy
questions.concept: They are particularly useful on the face, eyelids and flexures where prolonged steroid use causes atrophy and telangiectasia. Transient burning on application is the commonest side effect.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: The most reliable method of establishing personal identity is:
options: Fingerprints (dactylography), as they are unique and unchanging
questions.concept: Dermal ridge patterns form by the fourth month of fetal life, remain unchanged throughout life and are destroyed only by deep dermal damage. Loops are commonest, followed by whorls, arches and composites.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Age estimation in a living person aged 15 to 21 years relies chiefly on:
questions.concept: Ossification centres appear and epiphyses fuse in a predictable sequence, so radiographs of the wrist, elbow, shoulder and pelvis are used. Age assessment matters medico-legally for consent, criminal responsibility and marriage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Sex determination from skeletal remains is most reliable using:
options: The pelvis, followed by the skull
questions.concept: The female pelvis is broader with a wider subpubic angle above 90 degrees, a larger circular inlet and a wider greater sciatic notch. The pelvis gives about 95% accuracy, and with the skull about 98%.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: DNA fingerprinting for identity is best performed on:
options: Any nucleated cell source such as blood, hair root, bone or tissue
questions.concept: Mature erythrocytes lack nuclei, so DNA comes from leucocytes in blood. Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited and useful for degraded remains and hair shafts without roots.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: The Gustafson method estimates age from:
options: Age-related changes in teeth including attrition, secondary dentine and root resorption
questions.concept: Gustafson scores six dental parameters - attrition, periodontosis, secondary dentine, cementum apposition, root resorption and root transparency - each 0 to 3, and is applied to adults where epiphyses have fused.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Stature can be estimated from long bones using:
options: Regression formulae such as those of Trotter and Gleser, applied to the femur or tibia
questions.concept: Long bones of the lower limb correlate best with height. Formulae are population and sex specific, so applying Western formulae to Indian remains introduces error - hence Indian-specific tables are used.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Corpus delicti in forensic medicine refers to:
options: The essential facts constituting the crime, including identification of the body
questions.concept: Establishing identity of the deceased is a fundamental part of the corpus delicti, without which a charge of homicide cannot proceed - which is why identification is a core forensic responsibility.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Superimposition technique for identification involves:
options: Photographic or video comparison of a skull with an antemortem photograph of the suspected individual
questions.concept: Anatomical landmarks of the skull are superimposed on a life-size photograph. It is chiefly a method of exclusion rather than positive identification, and is used when other methods are unavailable.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: Tattoo marks are useful for identification but their limitation is that they:
options: Can be removed or altered, and pigment may spread to regional lymph nodes
questions.concept: Tattoos may be surgically or chemically removed leaving a scar, and are chosen so they may be shared by groups. Pigment in draining nodes can reveal a removed tattoo, and infrared photography may recover faded designs.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Identification: age, sex, dactylography, DNA, anthropometry
questions.stem: The Bertillon system of identification was based on:
options: Anthropometric body measurements, now superseded by fingerprinting
questions.concept: Bertillonage used a series of body measurements but was abandoned because measurements change with age and can coincide between individuals, unlike the unique and permanent fingerprint.
